Rear light and motor braking issues are solved:

# Motor phases were shorted to main frame from the Wye connection.
# The cobra wiring used had some floating wires in the wiring.
# The voltage that was “leaking” into the main frame caused all sorts of disturbances across the wiring and the floating wires only amplified these.
#  when the floating wires touched the main frame metal with their conductive parts, then this motor braking and rear light issue occurred. I was able to recreate this. Also tested with working motor and everything was OK. 
# If the motor is shorted to the main frame, then the rear light may be more illuminated when the scooter is driving. Used 1000pF capacitor to filter the noise from the rear light signal. This is something that should be included in the rear light by design I think. 

This issue was not related to the controller.

This is the biggest opening we can afford if we make the opening from the Handlebar through the Steerer Pole. The bottleneck will be where the brake hose will go into the Steerer Pole and the width is 25mm. 

The actual problem will be with the 55mm cut-out. This space needs to be shared by 2 brake hoses. Which means the radius per hose is around 27mm. 

If we make the cut-out height bigger like 55x14 then one brake hose be on the top and the other be on the bottom and have a large radius. In this scenario, the Handlebar will get weaker and more pressure will be on Handlebar Holders. 

!image-20230428-081246.png|width=1810,height=997!

I believe we can make the correct solution better with plastic modification and making the cut-out on the Steerer Pole longer towards the bottom.

Front light issue is solved - The newest hardware uses smaller value resistors to sample the light current than the samples that we have in hand. 

Speek is using older Cobra light, which has about 65mA of current draw at 24V and the newer “Dragon lights” are using about 40mA. Therefore, old resistor values in combination with new firmware create a measurement error of 67%. The current error is generated at 100mA - the measurement error creates the “Speek light” to exceed the threshold and therefore the error is generated. The new “Dragon light” does not exceed 100mA with this combination and therefore we have not noticed it before. Genfo has mentioned it in their firmware release notes and I have the latest schematic, so everything is alright.

We can just change these resistors in our current controller samples and everything will be OK. 

Old resistor value 51 Ohms

New resistor value 34 Ohms.

Brake issue was caused by two things: 

# The cable housing did not have end barrel on the lever side, *which are super important!* Without using end barrels, the end of the housing will get chewed up and it will get stuck in the brake lever body. See image.
# The cable housing was kinked where it exits the diagonal tube and goes into the side channel of the main frame. This is impossible to notice without pulling the housing out of the frame, as this part is completely hidden. The routing of this part is difficult, easy to damage the cable housing because of the tight turn there. Maybe it would be possible to slightly enlargen the cut in the side? It would help greatly. See image.

I replaced the cable housing, installed brand new housing end barrels and installed a brand new brake cable. I also installed the spring between the drum brake actuator, it will slightly improve the lever response. However I cut of a few coils from the spring as the original spring is too long and will make the brake harder to pull.

Range test result: 

* 75 km (bike computer). Calibrated on 200m distance before the test.
** 77,4 km Garmin GPS



* Normal city ride, tried to imitate normal client ride, avoid very long straight riding.
* Mostly max throttle or no throttle used
* Asphalt surface 99%
* Almost no high hills
* Rider about 70+ kg
* Scooter 26,7 kg
* Air temp 18°C first day and 10°C second day
* Battery disconnected between rides
* *100 to 0% battery.* Battery closed output in the end, SOC display 0%. *Before that power seemed decent.* Uphill speed just some minutes before end: 25 km/h - Pärnu mnt bridge over railway (59.41967175943892, 24.74186193694979).
* Acceleration current 20 used. Brake current 15.
* Max Power in log, with full battery: 950W (Cobra has about 800W)
* Max Power in log, with 1% SOC : 750W
* Tires 3 bar pressure before test
* Some thoughts about range:
** Range could be shorter when driven in city center
** Range could be longer when driven on flat ground, constant speed
** Acceleration current could be set lower, this would make range a bit longer 
* Rough calculation of distance lost, if we consider to keep IOT online after ride end:
** Cobra IOT uses about 24Wh per 24h
** Cobra battery is about 540 Wh
** Ops seem to use 10% as ride stopping value for client
** This leaves 540Wh*0,1=54 Wh of energy into battery, which is about 48h of IOT online time
** Dragon has about 1kw battery
** This means IOT online time 48h is possible with: 54Wh / 1000Wh = 5,4% SOC (Dragon)
** 5,4% SOC means 75km * 5,4 / 100 = 4 km

[~accountid:5f896ba2e357dd006e937e5b] Overview of the helmet lock

We had multiple [concept/ideas|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RNTL/pages/4570219503/D1+-+Helmet+lock] for the helmet lock and narrowed it down to two options:

# Aluminum extrusion with optimized shape, so there will be less milling
## *Mold cost:* *66400 RMB*
### Front (U-shape bracket): 57200 RMB
### Rear (lock base): 9200 RMB
## *Unit cost:* *21,4 RMB*
### Front (U-shape bracket): 11,6 RMB
### Rear (lock base): 9,8 RMB
## *Time:* 25 days to open tooling
# U shaped bracket the front side part is still aluminum extrusion but the Rear part where lock is attached is injection molded plastic
## *Mold cost:* *88200 RMB*
### Front (U-shape bracket): 57200 RMB
### Rear (lock base): 31000 RMB
## *Unit cost:* *14,75 RMB*
### Front (U-shape bracket): 11,6 RMB
### Rear (lock base): 3,15 RMB
## *Time:* 
### 25 days to open tooling for extrusion
### 40 days to open injection mould

Prices are provide by Minta and SS.

Since we must have these parts in Europe by the 1 December to have some time for up-fitting. Which at this point leaves us from today {{2023-10-11}} *51 days* to produce tooling, parts and ship them to Europe. 

Using injection mould we will have less than *10 day* to produce parts and ship them to EU, which will be very critical in time wise and will not leave no room for errors. Also initial investment to tooling is also notably bigger (+32%).

*Decision: It was decided to use extruded aluminum parts for helmet lock mounting because time line will be better and we will have ''room'' if there are some troubles.*

We had a meeting with Electrolube {{2023-06-27}} . The outcome of the discussions are:

* 2 out of 8 batches of UR5638 had a problem. One batch is defined as NG due to a cloudy finish when it cures and the other is due to a longer gel time. Both issues come from chemical reactions and Electrolube doesn’t suggest to use them.
* *To make the UR5638 less viscous, it can be heated up. We will ask what is the viscosity at what temperature. Also, the nominal temperature and humidity of the potting environment will be re-asked.*

EPDM cannot be produced by injection molding. There are two kinds of process for it. One is foam process, one is vulcanization.

Foaming products are sheet-like. Hardness range: Shore C 20. other hardness needs to be customized, need a large MOQ.

Vulcanized products can have a 3D structure. Hardness range: Shore A 40~90. more expensive.

# Both burnt-out controllers have one chip capacitor burnt out, and the two chip capacitors are located in different positions
# The software engineer first conducted an analysis and suspected that a short circuit was causing it. They simulated a short circuit on the sample, but the chip came with a short circuit protection function, which immediately protected the chip from a short circuit and could not be replicated.
# Suspected to be regen current, but from the log, no abnormalities were found. However, the simulation was still conducted on the bench, and the charging function of the large battery was turned off. When the Regen voltage exceeded 62V, the controller immediately activated the protection.
# The hardware engineer also conducted an analysis and suspected that it was caused by SMT capacitors. They have already had cases from other customers where the same problem occurred due to improper PCB transportation, resulting in capacitor damage. They are trying to reproduce it now.

*Admin vehicle link:* [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-micromobility/vehicles/list/edit/rentalglobal/579186?tab=details|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-micromobility/vehicles/list/edit/rentalglobal/579186?tab=details]

The hatch was open, and 3PL was asked to collect it. Tht 3PL manager collected it and investigated.

*Their report:* _The battery hatch did not correctly lock - the hatch seemingly locked, but popped open at a random time later, just as if it was being released from some tension. The lock motor did not make any noise whatsoever. Having removed the battery, we discovered a plastic piece underneath the battery, which was lifting the battery higher than usual. We removed this plastic piece, and then the hatch locked properly and did not pop back open._

*Pictures:*

Hatch open on the street

!20230817_191603.jpg|width=50%!



Plastic piece, that was found under the battery (looks like spacer fitted during brake lever assembly in CN)

!File.jpg|width=50%!



Plastic piece location in the scooter

!368593717_1238434383485610_2446520543977027124_n.jpg|width=1536,height=2048!



*To conclude:*

Based on this information, the situation can be a combination of the lock cable end restricting complete movement, and extra debris under battery creating the perfect moment of tension, where the lock seemingly holds, but does not permanently fasten it to the scooter, so it pops open when the stress holding it together is relieved.

Yiyo conducted some tests, which can be briefly described as follows:
The pull-out force of the dust plug is 1100N, and the interference fit is 2mm;
Conduct fatigue testing on the front fork and check the dust plug every 200k times, the target is 1 million times：

# A little lubricating oil, no air cooling. The dust plug came off  at 200K checkpoint;
# Normal amount of lubricating oil with air cooling. The dust plug has not come off after 1 million times;

Yiyo‘s conclusion：

1: It may be due to the high temperature causing the lubricating oil to evaporate, resulting in the plug falling off

2: Suspension requires regular addition of white grease for maintenance

3: Future orders:

* Our front fork lubricating grease has been changed to self lubricating white oil with weak vaporization and high-temperature resistance
* Thickening the inner edge of the dust plug increases the pulling force, and increasing the reverse R angle at the lip reduces the reverse friction force

In some cases, the helmet lock (which is on the same 24V line as the IOT & AI module) fails to boot properly. The repetitive INIT failure is resulting in error frames on CANbus, which disrupts CANbus communication for short period of time. This also affects other devices on the CANbus (BMS, IOT, Controller). Thorough research in the report document.

h3. Bolt’s in-house workaround/mitigation by IOT & BMS FW

BMS FW(0013) was improved to behave in a more rugged way and not end the CAN communication in case of CAN error frames. This was implemented to avoid BMS init failures & in general improve the CANbus logic of the BMS.

Current init. fail loop can be worked around by disabling battery output for ~10s and re-enabling it. Currently, the IOT (fw. 3.27 ->) sends a message to the BMS in situations where helmet lock init. fails so that BMS can disable the output. IOT defines for how long the output shall be disabled (variable). The 10sec reset does not work 100% of the time - some helmet locks keep having the E10 condition (helmet lock init. failed). If the issue persist after the BMS output is restarted with a delay, then IOT will retry the process 2 more times, currently the IOT will behave as follows:

* 1. time - output disabled for 10 seconds, re-enable output
* 2. time - output disabled for 10 seconds, re-enable output
* 3. time - output disabled for 10 seconds, re-enable output

To mitigate the issue where some helmet locks still keep failing init after multiple 10s restarts, Aare is creating a patch to see if there is a difference in behavior when prolonging the disabled output period. IOT would behave as follows:

* 1. time - output disabled for 20 seconds, re-enable output
* 2. time - output disabled for 40 seconds, re-enable output
* 3. time - output disabled for 60 seconds, re-enable output

Initial tests for the final implementation, for locks which keep failing consistently, shows no hope for improvement, so it is possible that in these cases the locks are faulty.

h3. Helmet lock manufacturer cooperation regarding the issue

The manufacturer (Yueci) was sent the whole electrical setup of the vehicle, but they claim that they are unable to recreate the issue. Mr. [~accountid:6215e9f275803500683497d5] has tested with various components in HQ (Helmet locks which never showed signs of bad behavior) and was able to recreate this issue.

The supplier shall be held accountable for this, but to do this we must make it clear to them that the evidence is available and the issue can be simply recreated. Yueci claims that all should be fine, but it is clear that helmet locks are creating these issues consistently in our operational fleet.

The helmet lock E10 consistent state was possible to achieve by disconnecting & reconnecting the main battery multiple times consecutively (plug battery in, listen & determine if the helmet lock manages to init and try again if it succeeds, until it goes into this failure mode).

h3. Actions:

Take action against the Helmet lock manufacturer to make them act more critical about this kind of issue.

[~accountid:5e9a112618b8ed0c0f776390] to find out how we can get actionable data to build a case:

* What % of fleet experiences these kinds of helmet lock issues on a daily basis?
* What % of fleet experiences the helmet lock issues where we can’t help with the IOT FW workaround (helmet lock stays in faulty state)?

After gathering data, we shall agree with SCM to agree on how to proceed with Yueci regarding this issue.

*1st phenomena:* The reason of why the adapters shake/move relative to the rivets - it is clear and we agree - it is a design flaw due to the elliptical holes on the plastics.

*2nd phenomena:* Why the charging adapters can spin around the steerer pole and move upwards-downwards, that is another topic - the rivets do not seem to be long enough and are coming out of their sockets on the steerer pole.

We have tested with 3.2 x 10 (and bigger) aluminum rivets in Tallinn, and they do not cause the second phenomena at all. The adapter still moves/shakes, but the rivets will not come out of their sockets or break.

We tested with 3.2 x 8 rivets today, the rivets are not completely fastening the adapter plastic, as the rivet body just expands in the rivet hole - it can not reach the inside of the steerer pole. This exact situation is what we are experiencing in all markets currently.

h3. Brussels defective locks report

Brussels sent 8 of 10 requested D1.08 & D1.11 locks to HQ for investigation. Results:  [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1aqD3sCdZ53ObKBYBvO9r1D1Jot5xk1f-dwlwreuknO8/edit?gid=0#gid=0|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1aqD3sCdZ53ObKBYBvO9r1D1Jot5xk1f-dwlwreuknO8/edit?gid=0#gid=0|smart-link] 

Here is a report about the issues:

# *Emergency release cable issue*: All of the locks, which were possible to be disassembled & reassembled (not too damaged, 7/8 in total), had issues with lock popping open when bending the housing. 
## How it was tested:
### Locking the lock with a screwdriver, then bending the release cable housing - if lock pops open, test fails
### Before locking the lock, the release cable housing was slightly bent, and then the lock was locked with a screwdriver. After locking, the screwdriver was pulled towards the “open” position - if lock pops open, test fails
###* *_All tested (& working) locks failed both of these tests_*
## (i) According to current spec, the tolerance between the cable tip ball & cable housing edge is 53 + 2 mm, so 53-55 mm. Out of 8 locks, 3 were in tolerance & in spec. *_Nevertheless_* all locks suffered from the same phenomena.
## (i) Out of 8 locks, 4 had slight signs of vandalism.
## *Conclusion:* issue with cable lock was reproducible with all locks which were sent to us.



# *Locking latch deformation issue*: out of 8 locks, 5 had deformed locking latch tips
## All locks were disassembled and checked on the inside
## It appears that the material is soft enough that the external pulling force of the Dragon hatch (when being vandalized/pried open) is able to completely deform the locking latch.
### Reports of different deformation levels:
### No deformation - {color:#006644}*Good lock latch*{color}
!IMG20240812134106.jpg|width=3072,height=4096,alt="IMG20240812134106.jpg"!
### Slight deformation - {color:#6554c0}*NOK lock latch*{color}
!IMG20240812130115.jpg|width=3072,height=4096,alt="IMG20240812130115.jpg"!
### Medium deformation - {color:#ff991f}*Bad lock latch*{color}
!IMG20240812125024.jpg|width=3072,height=4096,alt="IMG20240812125024.jpg"!
### Extreme deformation - {color:#ff5630}*Very bad lock latch*{color}
!IMG20240812134944.jpg|width=3072,height=4096,alt="IMG20240812134944.jpg"!
## (i) In such situations, the lock was still possible to lock, but the worse the deformation was, the more difficult it was to lock, as more force was required to push.
## (x) This deformation is unacceptable, since we do not see if it has happened and it could cause also this 50-50% situation, where the hatch stays *_seemingly_* in a locked position, but when pulled with enough force, it pops open.
## *Key takeaways:* The latch material is either unspecified, not according to specification or the design/shape is insufficient. We need to change the design, material or both.



# *Lack of grease around moving parts* (small issue) - there was grease applied only here the two latches meet, but there are much more moving parts which would benefit from added grease (pivot points for latches, lock motor & locking latch connection point) to avoid seizure & dirt/water clogging the moving parts. Inexpensive to add during assembly.
## (i) This is just a discovery and a remark, nothing to do with the issue at hand.

*Different rivets*

The test was conducted, as in the rivet catalog the specified “thickness of the material to be riveted” for the 3.2 x 10 mm aluminum rivet as 5.5-7 mm. From the Dragon model, I measured more than 7.5mm of the total thickness for adapter fastening. My assumption was, that the rivet wasn’t long/big enough, so before doing the double-riveting method, different rivets were tested:

* 3.2 x 12 mm aluminum rivet
* 3.2 x 14 mm aluminum rivet
* 3.2 x 16 mm aluminum rivet
* 4 x 12 mm aluminum rivet (with 4.1 mm hole)

All of the rivets yielded same results, the adapter moved similarly in each situation. The overlapping plastic holes are still too oval, and will allow play in forward/backward positions regardless on how the rivet pulls it against the material.

*Problem on the first mass produced D1 adapters which were installed on the first scooter batch in Riga.* It`s possible to install and rivet parts tightly close to each other and it stays like that placed properly but it gets loose if the front tip of the adapter is pressed down or pulled up. It gets loose because of the oval-shaped rivet hole in the front part of the adapter as it was assumed. Oval shaped hole just makes sliding possible. Rivet size, if it`s 3.2x10 aluminum is not causing it. For the next adapters batch, the injection mold needs to be modified but for the quick fix this one below could be an option.

Additional rivets is the best quick fix to implement in the warehouse.

I did pre-testing (for getting familiar to that device and to plan upcoming testing) with “random” PTC fuse from dock IOT circuit board:

* PolySwitch nanoASMDCH016F [https://www.littelfuse.com/~/media/electronics/product_specifications/resettable_ptcs/littelfuse_ptc_nanoasmdch016f_product_specification.pdf.pdf|https://www.littelfuse.com/~/media/electronics/product_specifications/resettable_ptcs/littelfuse_ptc_nanoasmdch016f_product_specification.pdf.pdf]
* !image-20221229-203040.png|width=816,height=200!

Wires were soldered to PTC and temperature sensor attached to it with electrical tape. PTC thermal conditions were now a bit more like in real wiring harness.

!image-20221229-203336.png|width=33.33333333333333%!

Constant current power supply was used and stabilized temperature reading noted. Room temperature 22 °C:

!image-20221229-204112.png|width=16.666666666666664%!

!image-20221229-204013.png|width=41.666666666666664%!

338mA was highest temperature to stabilize without tripping 

Tripping event, 368mA, PTC fuse already hot, after tripping: 27V (max by supply), 23mA:

!image-20221229-204600.png|width=782,height=529!

Temperature peaked to 150°C and stabilized at 100°C

Tripping event, 368mA, PTC starting from room temperature:

!image-20221229-205132.png|width=726,height=498!

Temperature peaked to 100°C and stabilized 

Voltage drop measured with PTC at room temperature. Heat generation is higher with higher voltage drop:

!image-20221229-205352.png|width=50%!

Seems to be very linear relation

With constant current of 418 mA, voltage drop - PTC temperature relation was observed. Temperature was changing fast so results might not be very repeatable but still graph shape can be observed.

!image-20221229-205806.png|width=664,height=274!

After 75°C PTC tripped to high resistance (protection) state.

After short circuit (5,1A max by supply), PTC fuse works again. 

Conclusion:

* TRIPPED-STATE POWER DISSIPATION (in watts) might give some idea about max temperature for this component in wiring harness but at least this PTC datasheet does not have much info about thermal behavior.
* HOLD current value (not going to protective state) could be exceeded considerably in this test without fuse tripping.
* For next tests, with real candidates, I suggest:
*# Short circuit test with OKAI charger - check stabilized temperature, pass: <60°C
*# What is max current possible without tripping? Probably 1A-1,5A is good enough but possibility to have it even lower
*# Short circuit PTC after max current test (hot start) and assess results
*# 6A short circuit test, repeatedly, for reliablity
*# Would need diode samples to test - how hot will they get with 1A and 1.5A

So let me sum up my understanding of this solution here for myself so I won’t forget.

# Assemble the bottom nut and overtight it - until 35Nm? (So that the compression rings will settle down and all the gaps will be removed)
# Untighten the bottom nut - not fully but lower than 10Nm.
# *Tighten the bottom nut with 10Nm* (so that the inner ring of the bearing won’t be overloaded)
# Add a washer on top of the bottom nut
# *Tighten the top nut with 35Nm*

*Data about the package vibration test:*

*Equipment for vibration test:*

# 12 Bolt scooters.
# 3 sets of new packaging box.
# Vibration test machine.

 

*Test Method:*

# Pack all 12 Bolt scooters and 4 Bolt scooters per cartoon box.
# Place 3 cartoon box vertically on the machine, simulated how its set up in the container.
# Set the vibration frequency in 1.5-5.0 HZ
# Set the vibration amplitude in 25 millimeters.
# The direction of vibration is up and down/right to left repeatedly.
# Run the test for 240 minutes.

 

*Test Results* (Two subjects will be checked)

# The appearance of Bolt scooters.
# The functionality of Bolt scooters.

 

The appearance will be focus on if any scratches on the surface of scooters, as during the transportation, the scooters will possibly rub against the cartoon paper, if any scratches occurs, extra protection will be needed.

 

The functionality can be known after the assemblers install all the parts togethers;

My opinion is if the appearance of scooters or the cartoon box is good, there will not be problems of the functionality of scooters.

We made one more test where we added a washer under the bottom nut. It helps to avoid friction in between the bottom nut and spacer. It avoids torque reduction due to friction. But the problem with this setup is that the threaded tube doesn't come out if the top nut. So the top surface of the top nut is almost on the same lever as the top surface of the fork tube. Let's say if there is a torque reduction due to friction and it is lowered to 5Nm then the axial force will be more than 658N, which should eliminate all the possible gaps and fix the bearings.

Then I continued to compare the internals of the locks. C1 is completely different from Yueci and might not be a good comparison at the moment because it did not lock properly:

!image-20240905-125737.png|width=1021,height=707,alt="image-20240905-125737.png"!

But C2 and Dragon are so similar that I am quite sure they are *exactly the same*:



!image-20240905-125839.png|width=947,height=583,alt="image-20240905-125839.png"!

However on closer inspection you can see that the D1 lock internal mechanism is way lower quality. The latches match almost perfectly on the C2 lock, while they are very loose on D1.

!image-20240905-130436.png|width=1304,height=439,alt="image-20240905-130436.png"!



!image-20240905-130845.png|width=728,height=749,alt="image-20240905-130845.png"!

I believe this is big part of the reason we see that the lock is popping open. There is nothing that stops the longer lever to slide away from the short lever, while on the C2 lock the *tips of the levers interfere with each-other*. Also on the C2 unlocking requires that the hook (short lever) is *pulled slightly downwards by the long lever*. On the Dragon lock the long lever simply slides off with almost 0 friction.



Next test to be done on {{2024-09-06}}: find a way to extend the hook on the Dragon hatch or make it lock easier otherwise (by removing thickness of the rubber pads) and then repeat the hammering test. During the current test the C2 lock was under quite big tension from the hook and this might have also altered the results, so it is *too early for any conclusions.*

I disassembled both Depu and Wuxing brake levers and compated the internal structure:

* Wuxing uses bolt to secure lever blade to lever body; Depu uses a rivet. Bolt offers possibility to repave the lever blade in case it breaks and also adds the possibility to adjust the lever blade to reduce wobble.
** for testing purpose I took the bolt from Wuxing lever and installed it on Depu. The adjustment that the bolt provides gave made big difference in reducing the wobbly lever blade.
* There are plastic bushings inside both levers. On Wuxing the bushings are very tight fit. On the Depu lever the bushing fits decently to the axle of the lever blade (rivet), but it is very loose inside the lever blade. This could greatly improve the feeling if the bushings were precise.
* The anchor point of the cable is ~15% further away from the lever blade axle on the Wuxing lever, which provides additional leverage and more stopping power.

[~accountid:5e4658b55a495e0c91a7a011] and [~accountid:5e9a112618b8ed0c0f776390] did a disassembly test with Dragon scooter from Tallinn that had a loose fork. [~accountid:5e9a112618b8ed0c0f776390] [~accountid:5e4658b55a495e0c91a7a011] please describe your findings under this task:

The process for adjusting headset bearing fastening bolts can currently be done by:

* Releasing brake cables and the front brake cable housing from the zip-ties
* Removing diagonal tube cover plastic to check the cables when they are under tension throughout the process
* Removing the IOT top cap and disconnecting every single cable (front light, indicators, brake sensors, throttle etc.), which includes removing grips, brake levers, and everything else to have access to the connectors.
* Lifting the steerer pole upwards enough to get it over the spacer and adjustment nuts and setting it aside
* Adjusting the nuts so that the bearing is properly tensioned
* Reassembling

⏲️  The most time consuming part is dealing with components in the handlebar/IOT caps area, as it requires a lot of disassembly of the different aforementioned components to access cables and to later refit them. 

⚠️  The problem is that the steerer pole needs to be lifted upwards about 120 mm (100 mm spacer height + 2x8 mm nut height + few millimeters for clearance), which is a lot.

✔️  Undoing the brake cables and brake cable housings is not a very time consuming thing to do, and requires few components/fasteners to be removed, and this will allow for the brake actuating system to move upwards with the steerer pole itself.

(x) What is restricting the steerer tube/handlebar assembly to move upwards in this case are all the electrical cables. The cable lengths are currently insufficient in a way, that they get under too much tension and will unplug from some location or risk damage. The biggest concern is for the front wheel speed sensor, which is one-way cable from the sensor to the IOT, so there is no play there.

(/) What could be the solution for streamlining this process would be eliminating any work related to the IOT top cap/handlebar assy. and connecting cables, and eliminating that step altogether. This could be done by extending the cables in some way that they allow further vertical movement of the steerer pole/handlebar assy., or make the spacer shorter, so that the steerer pole/handlebar assy. wouldn’t have to be moved so high vertically.

Foam hardness is generally tested with Shore C hardness tester, because Shore C hardness tester needle is a round ball, measuring foam and other soft microporous materials,  the force surface is larger than Shore A tester needle, so the measured data error will be smaller. *Will save 50g*
*Down side:*
* it may affect the the water drainage because the water will stay into channels (the drainage holes are not in every channel so the water can not escape before the water level is higher than the height of the channel)|
| | |
|*OPTION 2: one wider channel on the bottom surface*| |
|!image-20230711-091801.png|width=1192,height=769!


*FEM: no change in FEM*
!image-20230711-125832.png|width=1359,height=783!|!image-20230711-091827.png|width=1226,height=601!
The width of the channel from the top edge is 100mm (with of the bottom edge is 90mm) and height 0.5mm
*Down side:*
* the front drainage holes do not work as effectively as they worked before because they are on the higher surface. 
* It is possible to change the position of the holes but there is a risk that someone will drill into the endcap of the battery and damage the battery
!image-20230711-092922.png|width=1058,height=525!
!image-20230712-100311.png|width=1242,height=553!

*Will save 60g*
This solution will not affect the water drainage but there is a risk that someone will drill into battery endcap and damage the battery !!!|
|*OPTION 3: one wider channel on the bottom surface + thinner side walls*


*FEM: no change in FEM*
!image-20230711-143732.png|width=1279,height=913!|!image-20230711-132056.png|width=1340,height=692!
!image-20230712-100258.png|width=1242,height=553!

*Down side:*
* the front drainage holes do not work as effectively as they worked before because they are on the higher surface. 
* It is possible to change the position of the holes but there is a risk that someone will drill into the endcap of the battery and damage the battery

*Will save 60g+160 g = 220g*
This solution will not affect the water drainage but there is a risk that someone will drill into battery endcap and damage the battery !!!|
|*OPTION 4: thinner side walls + opened motor cable channel + thinner outer upper corner*

*FEM: very small change in FEM*

With that solution we will loose 60g but the drainage holes can stay under the ribs and if someone wants to drill through the holes then we will not damage the battery. It is better to keep the battery safe and loose 60g than loose a battery.

*Will save 160 g + 90 g= 250g*|



*Conclusion:* *Option 4* is the best solution but needs a new extrusion mold because of so different changes + new PUSH / PULL  and DRUM test later

* After cutting the ribs narrower, there wasn’t interference anymore, but the noise didn’t disappear. Cutting it narrower doesn’t solve the issue or make the brake performance better, 
** Perhaps the assembly could get slightly better. 
* Even tho the brake hose and end cap are assembled correctly in the brake lever, the pull direction is under angle. 
** Due to this misalignment, the wire rubs against the strong end cap. 
** Moving or bending the brake hose won’t solve this issue. 
** The end cap is against the stopper feature in the brake lever. 

This issue might be coming from: 

# Due to tolerances in the brake lever 
# Due to the brake wire isn’t fixed in the middle of the wire-end-ball. 
# Due to the slot in the brake lever being under the wrong angle.

Comparison:

*FOS:*  2.6 (#Option 1) vs 1.9 (27% lower) (#Option 2) vs 2.1 (19% lower) (#Option 3)

*Max stress location:* same

*Stress over 60 MPa volume in frame:* 0.02% vs 0.03% vs 0.03%



*Conclusion:* Not to change the cut out size and shape but replace the metal spring tube to more flexible protection hose like heat shrink that is melted only from two ends but not from the center because in that case the cable can bend more easily. Or we could use also fabric tape that is used widely in car industry.

Verified that the issue is on the light side than on the controller side.

# Added capacitor between GND and transistor base which is switching on and off the brake mode - it had no effect, the light was still blinking
# Desoldered the transistor base pin from the PCB which is switching on and off the brake mode - It had no effect, the light was still blinking
# Desoldered the "Brake mode" wire from the controller PCB - The light was still blinking.
# Used external power supply to supply the rear light and the "brake" cable was left floating - when it touches the scooter metal frame, the light was blinking.
 Also, when touching the brake cable wire just by human hand, the rear light also lights up.
 Added 1 uF capacitor between the GND and "brake" wire. After this, when the brake wire touched the scooter frame, the light was not blinking.

Adding the capacitor seems to provide a return path for the unwanted signals that are generated to the "brake" wire.

h3. *Test guide:*

# Find and document the testing tracks. 
## Area with a *20-40mm curb step* (single direct impact vertically hand longitudinally)
## Certain section of *cobblestone road*
## Certain section of the *surface behind the office*
## The distance of either one should be *at least 100 meters long*
# Test conditions:
## Vehicle speed *20-25 km/h* (maximum throttle) - needs to be achieved before the testing track area
# Setting up vehicles and measurement devices
## Fix the two phones simultaneously to the handlebar and to the footboard.
## On both phones, run the Phyphox app, for recording method select “*Acceleration (without g)*”
# Run the test on the *cobblestone road*
## Just before the test (before accelerating towards the road section), click the “Play” triangle to start recording the accelerations *on both phones*.
## Conduct the ride across the section of road
## Click the “Pause” button (2 lines) to stop the recording.
## Click the on the 3-dot button in the right corner of the display, select “Export data”.
## For data format, select “*CSV (Comma, decmial point)*”. Click OK.
## Save with “File manager”. Select any folder in the internal memory, but remember the folder to later retrieve the data. Also note the order of tests (approximate times) so that the data can later be distinguished between different vehicles.
## Return to the app, clear the data by clicking on the “*Trash bin*” icon
## Repeat the test 2 more times with the same vehicle to get more samples of the test.
# Run the test on the *surface behind the office*
## Follow the same steps below Chapter 4.
# Run the test with the *20-40mm curb step*
## Follow the same steps below Chapter 4.

After testing has concluded, gather all the CSV logs to the computer and refer them to the tested vehicle, test condition and test sample number.

[~accountid:5e4658b55a495e0c91a7a011] opened the TWS battery:

* The gaskets are glued to the aluminum housing and the plastic caps. Done professionally, looks very good and it was sealed properly all around.

* The potting quality is perfect.
* The BMS is protected much better. It is covered with a layer of PC film on the top side that is taped down on the sides with the same kind of foam tape that Techsum uses, but on top of the foam layer they have used some additional plastic tape that keeps everything together. Again, looks professional.
* The potting quality is exceptional:
* there are no air pockets to be seen anywhere. Top cap is completely filled, every gap and crack is filled. (check picture)
* *the potting is mixed perfectly\!* The compound, when mixed properly, is actually different from what we have seen in (even the best) Techsum batteries. The potting material is completely dry, not sticky like in Techsum batteries. It is so dry that if you break it off the parts of the housing, it produces some dry dust that sticks to your hands. And it can be removed from the battery in quite big chunks. No need to even use the brush method [@martin.luts|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U039XAAGZMZ] Think trying to snap a piece of rubber eraser (for erasing pencil) in half vs play doh.
* There are no traces of transparent mystery goo anywhere inside the battery. No traces of unmixed A/B components. On one battery the PC film covering the BMS was very slightly oily to touch, but nothing like we see in Techsum battery.

Battery waterproof test report  from Techsum.

They made 3 times waterproof test:

# UV water under 1 meter for 24 hours → No water inside
# Vibration test 15H + UV water under 1 meter for 24 hours  → No water in, but cap are separated from the potting glue
# Thermal cycle test + UV water under 1 meter for 24 hours → Water inside.

*Conclusion:* Long time vibration test, will make the potting glue and cap separation, or even the potting glue has the possibility of cracking；
Long time thermal cycle test, make the upper and lower cap and rubber seal deformation, water can enter the inside of the battery.

So here are some things that I found when adding complexity.

* Adding not only Android, but also iOS costs. Setting the same GP for Android and iOS - example [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/?o=3829506390716583#notebook/2719352897333851/command/2719352897333852]
** Multiple cases where the model does not converge and gives divergencies. Even with most flexible Gaussian Processes.
** In cases where it converged, you do not really like the GP, it seems not to give much credibility - you do not just understand why the model decided to increase or decrease exactly at that time.
*** This problem might actually grow even bigger as we *add channel-level complexity* (i.e. the model will have so many degrees of freedom)
*** This leads me to idea of switching to proxy-metric (CTR, Attribution) research first. This would at least give some directional seasonality of how time-varying coefficients could develop - see [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH-6092]



*Note:* I am not saying just fitting the GP is impossible. I am just saying that it might be too random when done on its own (especially with multiple variables). 

*Note2:* There’s still room to explore technical opportunities to specify different models. But for now, the idea to do it without specific proxies does not allow any of them to seem productive.

# It is important that blocking is done in a non-discriminatory manner and therefore it would be good practice that you have a process to deal with these situations, involving the central fraud team. ##  with a statement of reasons for that decision, which should identify the grounds for the decision, based on the grounds that the provider had set out in advance in its terms and conditions, and refer in a proportionate manner to the relevant specific circumstances, including third party notifications, that led to that decision;
## the statement should be available on a durable medium (i.e. an email);

Hi [~accountid:62722e092db308007024a425] , Has blocking drivers for speeding been ever considered in terms of reclass risk? If so, can you please let me know what was the conclusion? 

I understand that speeding is a huge problem (overall) but in my opinion we should be careful about drawing consequences from such incidents due to the following (in terms of reclass risk):

# +Blocking of a driver due to speeding could be considered as a control of performance of driver’s services as in employment relationship+. Speeding is subject to criminal activity, therefore it is personal responsibility of the driver to abide by law (employer is not responsible for paying the fines etc.). 
Polish courts generally find that numerous +fines+ for speeding might be a reason for termination of the employment contract due to loss of “trust” in the employee, yet not in disciplinary proceedings. Here we would base our decision to block the driver not on fines but on data gathered by the app. As far as I am concerned we do not have any access to a register of fines imposed on drivers.
# +As a platform provider we are responsible for organizing the transport, not for its performance+, therefore I would consider Bolt’s blocking as too interfering.
# the Police in Poland can draw consequences for speeding only if the speed is measured with a specific device. If we use data in app to draw consequences for speeding, then +there is a risk that the driver will claim that the speed was measured wrongly+, app is not a speed-measurement device etc.

On the other hand, there is [P2B regulation|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1150/oj] that - notwithstanding the above - allows the platform to restrict, suspend or terminate the services for the driver and I do believe that if we are able to justify our decision to suspend/restrict or terminate the services taken as a result of speeding and to follow other requirements resulting from the regulation, then we are fine to block the driver.

A company has raised a complaint regarding the unauthorised use of one of their email address - [+*intersect@gmail.com*+|mailto:intersect@gmail.com] by a private individual. Specifically, the user’s invoices are being sent to the company's email address, even though Bolt does not even operate in the company’s country of establishment. h1. Scenario 1: (changing *DENY* decisions to *FINISH*)

at the checkpoint, we have 3 possible decisions:

* {{pass}} decision: cancels ride (price 0)
* {{paid}} decision: finishes ride (system price)
* {{deny}} decision: denies the cancellation request

since {{deny}} has higher priority than {{paid}}, if both trigger, we’ll reject the cancellation request. however, if we're already deciding to allow the cancel request and charge the system price, there's absolutely no reason to just deny it. I've updated the *deny* rule to not trigger if the same conditions of the *paid* rule are also true.

outcome: better userX (less churn) and more GMV (users get unstuck from orders and can order again)

From legal point of view we always recommend to start cooperation only once the agreement has been signed for several reasons, the main ones are:

* accounting - parties cannot process invoice payments properly without a signed contract, as it is needed for accounting purposes to serve as proof of the obligation to pay.
* legal protection and risks - a contract serves as a legally binding agreement. If one party fails to meet their commitments, the other has legal recourse to enforce the agreement and seek remedies. Without a signed contract, there is no clear understanding of which risks each party is responsible for. This could result in Bolt being unable to claim compensation for breaches by the partner or Bolt assuming liabilities that would otherwise be excluded under the agreement.

{code:sql}%sql
WITH events_extracted AS (
  SELECT 
    support_case_id,
    created,
    event_data,
    CAST(get_json_object(event_data, '$.type') AS STRING) AS event_type,
    CAST(get_json_object(event_data, '$.assignee_handle.assignee_user_id') AS BIGINT) AS assignee_user_id,
    created AS event_created
  FROM ng_customer_support_spark.support_case_event
  WHERE event_type IN ('agent_added_internal_reply', 'escalated_to_agent')
  AND created > '2024-07-01'
)

-- Select cases where 'agent_added_internal_reply' happens before 'escalated_to_agent'
SELECT count(DISTINCT e1.support_case_id)
FROM events_extracted e1
JOIN events_extracted e2 
  ON e1.support_case_id = e2.support_case_id 
  AND e1.event_type = 'agent_added_internal_reply'
  AND e2.event_type = 'escalated_to_agent'
  AND e1.event_created < e2.event_created
  AND e1.assignee_user_id != 19039{code}

*Insights from as-is process map:*

* Asking the driver to wait for 5-15min doesn’t work, because:
** The driver is probably already waiting for some time while they wrote a message to CS
** There’s no live support, CS might get to that ticket way later, or even the next day.
* The process should be divided to 2 scenarios:
** Ongoing order - when CS picked up a ticket and the situation is happening currently
** Older order - when the situation happened some time ago
* For ongoing orders, CS should try calling the rider right away, and driver should keep calling the recipient in the meantime.
** *If nobody is picking up the phone:* the driver should drop the item at the certain spot (police station, office, etc..)
** *If the rider picks up the phone:* they should agree with the driver that driver will bring the item back to the rider. 
* For older orders, process could look like the 🚗[ *Driver: I found an item in the vehicle*|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/83740?country=global&language=en], where the driver just brings the item to the designated place.
* Price reviews: should be clarified better, that driver needs to finish the ride, submit the PR and then in the ticket give all the info on extra time spent and mileage covered. CS will close the PR with recalculated price only when the situation is resolved.
* Ukraine: option to send the parcel via post at rider’s expense. Looks too complicated and drivers probably are not willing to spend their time on it. Better just to drop the item at the designated place.

Hi [~accountid:62bff85c118b20bee2bdca35]!

When *tax* authorities request information to Bolt France, we do not provide any information. Instead, we just use this type of reply: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EPDyqWWLZWMUDXbo4gh67U1TCEsgMVnQIm78vGGneHY?usp=drive_fs|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EPDyqWWLZWMUDXbo4gh67U1TCEsgMVnQIm78vGGneHY?usp=drive_fs] 

For requests from other authorities, it's your discretion whether to cooperate. If we do, it's crucial from a tax perspective to clearly distinguish the roles of Bolt France and Bolt Operations.

In France, we operate under a centralized model, meaning that Bolt Operations (Bolt Ops) manages the business, signs the T&Cs with clients, and holds the authority to access their information. Bolt France is not legally responsible and should not provide driver data.

When clarifying the roles, I recommend asking the authorities to resubmit their requests to Bolt Ops OU at its Estonian office. The local team can then assist in preparing the information but only as a support function.

Additionally, all replies should be sent from Bolt Ops letterheads and never signed by local teams, to reduce visibility and minimize tax risks, especially around permanent establishment concerns that arise if a local employee signs on behalf of Bolt Ops.

By following these steps, we mitigate risks associated with local teams acting on behalf of Bolt Ops.

Does this work for you?

Hi [~accountid:712020:0b672045-ccee-47bd-a209-1bec8346b45c] - apologies for the delay while I was OOO. 

I have now had a chance to review EY’s comments and note that EY is pushing back on entering into a separate DSA on the grounds that “_The EY General Terms and Conditions (part of the agreement provided) already contain the clauses regarding data processing by EY as an operator_”. My comments on this are below. 

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*In summary*: I would still recommend pushing for a DSA. Given the value of the transaction, it is ultimately a business decision whether this is a hill that we want to die on. However given that: (1) we are sharing relatively sensitive employee information with both EY and GAC; and (2) the current agreement with EY does not contain certain protections that we would ordinarily push for, we should ensure that Bolt’s position is properly protected by implementing the DSA I previously prepared.
{panel}

*More detailed thoughts:*

* As EY will be acting as an independent controller under this arrangement, EY is correct that a DSA is *not* *_strictly_* *required*, as it is not mandatory to implement one under the GDPR. However, as standard practice, we typically push for a DSA to be implemented to *protect Bolt’s position* when we are sharing personal data with third parties.
* I have reviewed EY’s General T&C and they contain some very brief data protection provisions (at Clauses 21-23) - the only material obligation that these include is to require EY to comply with applicable data protection laws. *This falls short of the protections that we typically include on our standard form DSA*. In particular, our DSA requires EY to *indemnify* Bolt for any failures to adhere to data protection requirements - this is missing from EY’s General T&C, and is important for ensuring that our bases are covered.
* Beyond the pro-Bolt indemnity and a few additional standard terms that we include for practical reasons (e.g., a requirement for EY to notify Bolt of any relevant personal data breaches within 48 hours), our DSA does not contain any particularly burdensome / additional obligations for EY to adhere to. As such, *entering into the DSA should not necessarily be controversial for EY*.
* The employee data that we are sharing with EY is relatively *sensitive* (particularly with regards to salaries). Additionally, EY will be sharing this data with *GAC*, with whom Bolt does not have a direct contractual relationship. Both of these factors strengthen the case for ensuring that more fulsome contractual protections are in place in relation to Bolt sharing the data with EY.

*Next steps*

* I have made some minor updates to the [DSA|https://docs.google.com/document/d/18k83eL5jluKdgbMlVRGRCKdk3h1WMeWvSDkQle4lMsg/edit] to: (1) reflect the full list of categories of personal data that EY has highlighted; and (2) more clearly explain to EY why the provisions are either important to us or uncontroversial.
* Please could you *share the updated version of the DSA with EY* and again push for them to review / agree to it? When doing so, please feel free to flag the following:
** We appreciate that a DSA is not strictly mandatory, and that certain data protection obligations are already included in EY’s General Terms & Conditions. However, the EY T&Cs do not include certain provisions that we require to ensure that Bolt is adequately protected from a data protection perspective. Given the sensitivity of the data being shared, it is commercially reasonable for us to ask EY to enter into the DSA. We also note that many of the terms in our draft DSA should be relatively uncontroversial for EY.
** We have updated the DSA to reflect the full list of personal data that will be shared, and included more detailed explanatory comments for EY’s benefit throughout the draft. EY should review the DSA and let us know if they have any comments or concerns, which we can discuss.
* If EY continue to push back, then we can discuss how best to proceed. Given the overall value of the transaction, it is ultimately a business decision on whether Bolt is willing to proceed with this arrangement without a DSA. If we do not, then Bolt will need to accept the risk of not having our usual contractual protections in place - in particular, a pro-Bolt indemnity.
* Let me know if you have any questions on this! 🙂

Hi Anni, 

Thank you for your feedback and action on this matter.

This issue primarily relates to data integrity and accurate representation of driver status for consistency across the system. Currently, when a Partner-Level or Scheduled/Manual block is applied, the driver’s status remains _“Active,”_ which creates an operational pain point. As a result, we need to manually check the profile to verify the account’s true status. This can be especially problematic when the driver has been terminated due to Safety or Fraud concerns, as we believe the status should reflect the account’s permanent termination.

As you rightly pointed out, a termination decision is/ should be irreversible, thus, leaving the status as _“Active”_ undermines this decision + leaves us processing incorrect dates for Active Drivers. Both Central Compliance and Efficiency teams share the same view that we need to assess the handling of statuses for permanently blocked / terminated accounts.

There is an ongoing conversation with Product to address this, and a request has already been made to review this as part of the Global Blocking Project.

Hi Team, 

My thoughts on who should hard-block: 

While I understand the value of having a second pair of eyes on these cases to ensure quality, I believe that, given the behavior patterns we've observed from these perpetrators, swift action is critical. We've seen cases where one rider can harm or rob up to 5 drivers in a single night, often using multiple accounts on the same device. If we were to shift the responsibility for hard-blocking to the SIMs, the added review process could cause delays in restricting access, leaving us exposed to the risk of another driver being harmed by the same individual.

With how we propose to structure the investigation process, it is highly specific and detailed enough for the agent to make a sound judgment. This gives us an almost 95% chance of catching an actual perpetrator, reducing the likelihood of errors. Given this level of accuracy, I would suggest that the responsibility for hard-blocking remain with the BPO Safety Specialist processing the ticket to ensure swift action. Perhaps we could also implement a post-block review by the SIMs to provide additional oversight if needed.

 🙏

Successfully increased for M machines from 4 up to 6, using more parallel sessions slows down the tests due to CPU spikes:
	- Provider (one tests timing out with 20 min timeout, results are unreliable):
		- 4 parallel workers: CPU usage = avg. 39%, RAM usage = ~83%. Tests run time: ~28min/run/runner
		- 6 parallel workers: CPU usage = avg. 65%, RAM usage = ~84%. Tests run time: ~23min/run/runner
		- 8 parallel workers: CPU usage = avg. 70% (spikes up to ~99%), RAM usage = ~87%. Tests run time: ~29min/run/runner
	- Courier:
		- 4 parallel workers: ~45min/run/runner
		- 6 parallel workers: ~32min/run/runner
		- 7 parallel workers: ~39min/run/runner
		- 8 parallel workers: Possible CPU starvation/throttling, runner shut down, not reliable. ~48min/run/runner
	- Run times are approximate based on one run results, they may vary based on number of failed tests and prelive stability during the time tests were performed.

Provider 8 parallel workers average CPU usage shows insignificant increase compared to 6 parallel workers, but my assumption is that at the end there remains only one running test, which is timing out with 20 minutes timeout, making average number not very reliable. On courier side - 8 parallel workers tests showed flaky results, sometimes leading to CPU starvation and as a result - runner unresponsiveness. Most optimal variant is to use 6 parallel workers, as it seems most stable and gives us at least some increase in terms of tests execution speed.

In light of Zoom’s resistance to accepting changes, I have stripped back to volume of proposed edits and have only left those in where: (a) the inclusions are mandatory under data protection law; and/or (b) the inclusions are of particular importance to Bolt (given that this is an important contract for Bolt). The edits include explanatory comments for Zoom’s attention. {color:#4c9aff}*I would be more than happy to hop on a call with Zoom*{color} to discuss the revised edits if they are still not willing to accept them - just let me know. 

One point of particular importance to flag - the most essential inclusion for us is Clause 14 (the {color:#ff5630}*indemnity*{color} point) - we very rarely accept not including such an indemnity, particularly for such a key contract, and so {color:#ff5630}*we should push back on this as much as possible*{color}. This is because:

* As the controller, Bolt is generally accountable for the actions of its processors (i.e., Zoom). As such, Bolt must ensure it is contractually protected in the event that Zoom’s non-compliance with data protection laws results in regulatory action against Bolt. Neither the MSA nor DPA contains such an indemnity.
* Given that a data protection regulator could fine Bolt up to EUR 20m / 4% of worldwide turnover, we also cannot accept a liability cap of 240k for data protection breaches. If Zoom continues to push back on this point, we could accept a liability cap of 1 million Euros per claim (but this should not be shared with Zoom yet).

For good measure, I have also included my comments in the MSA ([https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lAGjQl_6OlME7cMhZmB1RmkUmwSbySKG/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lAGjQl_6OlME7cMhZmB1RmkUmwSbySKG/edit|smart-link]). Happy to discuss! 🙂

Dear Gerda Ordienė

 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *22 July 2024.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Balance reports* 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en/legal/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,



Bolt

Hi, we discussed the topic of DQO with product team, I recently posted it in: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C01U7BUQN0G/p1726473253997059?thread_ts=1722956854.625269&cid=C01U7BUQN0G|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C01U7BUQN0G/p1726473253997059?thread_ts=1722956854.625269&cid=C01U7BUQN0G|smart-link] 



Summarizing privacy POV below:



So, from Privacy POV, here are the main points to have in mind before launching DQO:

* As discussed previously in [#driver-prioritization-workgroup|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C051K1C57KJ], we raised a point that DQO is a tricky feature, especially since it might fall under the scope of "automated decision making" (ADM) under GDPR.
** In short, ADM is prohibited when there's an automated decision that causes significant effect to the driver and there's no human review.
** More information on what ADM is can be found [*here*|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4797989572/Understanding+Automated+Decision-Making+ADM].
* We did perform an analysis on whether DQO is *ADM and has significant effect:*
* From privacy POV, DQO will be a prohibited activity if it has significant effect (e.g. loss of substantial amount of earnings). If we prove there's no significant effect in the context of this specific feature - we can launch it.
** To see whether we can make this fall outside the scope of ADM, we asked the team to perform regular checks during the testing phase to see whether DQO causes the drivers to lose a significant amount of trips/earnings due to deprioritization.
*** In case the test would show that the drivers lose a significant amount of money due to DQO, we shouldn't launch it in that country.
*** *I am not aware of the latest results per country/city, so I'd kindly ask you to check each country before launch.*

* We can launch in markets where tests show no significant effect, keeping it outside the scope of ADM.

Szanowni Państwo,

 

W czerwcu i lipcu bieżącego roku przeprowadziliśmy audyt bezpieczeństwa pożarowego na terenie Norblin Industrial Park. Poniżej wnioski dotyczące spółki Bolt Services PL.

 

# Brak projektu powykonawczego dla prac wykonanych w rozdzielni RS2 w czerwcu i lipcu 2022 r. (przypominamy, że zgoda wydana w dniu 10 czerwca 2022 r. była uwarunkowana przedstawieniem stosownego projektu).
# Brak procedury związanej z samą instalacją ładującą baterie. Zdarzenia opisane w materiałach otrzymanych od Państwa dotyczą tylko baterii.
# Brak badania termowizyjnego instalacji elektrycznej zaleconego we wrześniu 2023 r. i powtarzanego w kolejnych latach.
# Brak informacji o wykonaniu zaleceń ppoż. zawartych w mailu z dnia 2 listopada 2022 dotyczących uszczelnienia przejść kablowych przez ściany oddzielenia pożarowego oraz wykonania systemu wczesnej detekcji dymu w obszarze ładowania baterii hulajnóg elektrycznych.
# Brak projektu wykonawczego dla monitoringu.

 

W związku z powyższym *wzywamy Państwa do uzupełnienia braków w dokumentacji w terminie do dnia 19 września br*. Hi [~accountid:712020:714baa0e-ddd0-4776-8064-c5a5d3ae37aa] 

The terms of the licence agreement are mostly reasonable and there are only a few clauses that could be clearer/more mutually beneficial. However, given (1) the urgency to have this contract in place; (2) the value of the contract being low; and (3) the fact that we’re unlikely to get them to change their standard terms for us, I’m only going to focus on the most important risks and how these can be mitigated without changing the terms. 

# *Deposit* - Can you please confirm the size of the deposit we will pay them. The licence agreement provides them with a lot of discretion in terms of how the deposit might be utilised. Thus, it would be helpful to know the size of the deposit (if any). 
# *Safeprotect* - Are we sure we want to opt in for storeprotect as opposed to taking our own insurance cover for the furniture? Storeprotect only covers a limited amount of things. For example, Safestore will not be liable for any damage to the furniture (e.g. damage caused by fire), which did not arise as a result of some fault on the part of Safestore or was not otherwise a damage that could have been reasonably anticipated by Safestore. Also, Safestore would retain full discretion as whether to repair or replace furniture in the event of damage (whichever is cheaper). However, if the furniture depreciates in value due to a repair carried out by Safestore, we have no recourse against Safestore. Thus, it might make more sense to cancel safeprotect and take out a separate insurance cover later on. Depending on the cost, it might even make sense to have both in place if there is a limited overlap between the two covers. 
# *Term* - I understand that we'll need to use this storage for at least 12 months since the contract cannot be terminated any earlier than September 2025. However, if we’re not sure if we will need this storage for the entire 12 month period, it might make more sense to ask for a rolling contract as opposed to 12 month fixed contract.
# *Delivery / Collection* - Who will cary out the collection/delivery of the furniture? The licence agreement provides that Safestore will not accept any liability for the damage to the goods during delivery/collection. This is quite important since goods in transit would be subject to a higher risk of damage. 
# *Liability* - we would be liable to Safestore for any losses incurred by them as a result of our use of the unit, any breach of licence terms/applicable regulations. Given the nature and value of the agreement, I don’t think we would be able to get them to change this or otherwise allow us to cap our liability. However, a separate insurance cover for goods could potentially mitigate this risk. Thus, I recommend that we look into this.

Common denominators in the orders → small driver distance & duration, but many times higher end price. Hence, we can compare the actual vs predicted pricing and decide if to return to metered instead. Aim is to cover these extreme examples of cases where we charge driver significantly higher for commission. Returning to metered pricing is a solution in order to price the ride correctly. This means that trips that are very short in time and distance (RDNH) (less than 200m and 3 min) should be excluded as a 0 pricing would be much more appropriate for these. 

I can see that majority of cases where duration and distance are half of what has been recorded (past 30 days) are small pricing issue with low impact (kes currency) and as we have very little information to tackle these accurately, we can opt for the more high priced and impactful cases where the pricing is over 2000 kes (13 eur).

Hi [~accountid:6346640e3f4224a46db29624], as you may recap, in Thailand, tax invoice must contain the wording in EN “Tax Invoice” or in Thai “ใบกำกับภาษี”.  This was communicated during launch and the details of tax invoice requirement is documented here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gX7jsVuKTQnUgZAy4TJWEihqp2WuFYyeqI7prt7JYsQ/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gX7jsVuKTQnUgZAy4TJWEihqp2WuFYyeqI7prt7JYsQ/edit|smart-link] 

In this case, the B4B Service fee invoice is a tax invoice.  It is correctly named “ใบกำกับภาษี” in Thai (same as the testing result, [thread here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05G86JS93R/p1695995711335459?thread_ts=1695989103.296099&cid=C05G86JS93R]).  If it is translated to EN, the title should be “Tax Invoice” as well.  

Similarly for commission invoices.  We also commented *“ใบแจ้งหนี้/ใบกำกับภาษี/ใบเสร็จรับเงิน*” and *"Invoice/Tax invoice/Receipt"* should be shown.  

Would we double-check if the Thai and ENG are aligned for other documents in Thailand as well if both Thai and ENG versions exist?  Thank you.

So this clause (see screenshot below) imposes an obligation of insurance and there are 2 alternative ways of compliance with the clause

# Bolt obtains an all-risk property insurance coverage for the assets (this cover will protect the assets from fire, theft, vandalism, flooding, earthquakes, etc.) 
# Bolt opt-ins for “StoreProtect” which increases the LLs liability from 100£ to the value of our property. However, this option will cover only the damages that the LL is liable for, so fire, theft, vandalism…  is generally not covered, the cover would only apply if the LL has not been duly diligent, e.g. fire alarm, theft alarm, etc. was not installed properly / not working. Furthermore, looking at the conditions of this StoreProtect scheme, it’s very unfavourable towards us and much more favourable towards the LL.
